title: Multicellular Organisms: Exchange and Transport Systems
seo_title: Year 11 Biology: Multicellular Organisms Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Cell specialisation and the levels of organisation; exchange surfaces; gas exchange, digestion and circulation in animals; the heart and blood vessels; transport of water and sugars in plants (xylem, phloem and transpiration). (Senior Secondary Biology, Unit 2: Cells and multicellular organisms)
meta_desc: Free Year 11 Biology worksheets on multicellular organisms: specialised cells, gas exchange, digestion, the heart and circulation, cardiac output, xylem, phloem and transpiration. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Big organisms need exchange surfaces and transport systems.
key_sub: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate.
body_html:
How to think about it

Multicellular organisms have specialised cells organised into tissues, organs and systems. Their small surface area to volume ratio means they need large exchange surfaces (alveoli, villi, root hairs, leaves) and transport systems.

In mammals the heart pumps blood in a double circulation; arteries carry it at high pressure, capillaries exchange materials and veins (with valves) return it. In plants, xylem carries water pulled up by transpiration and phloem carries sugars.

Example

Stroke volume 70 mL, heart rate 72 beats/min. Cardiac output?

70 × 72 = 5040 mL/min

Answer: 5.04 L/min

Example

Tidal volume 0.5 L, 15 breaths per minute. Ventilation rate?

0.5 × 15

Answer: 7.5 L/min

Common mistakes

  • Saying arteries carry oxygenated blood and veins deoxygenated: the pulmonary vessels are the other way round.
  • Thinking xylem carries sugar: that is phloem.
  • Forgetting that plants exchange gases through stomata, not only by diffusion through the whole leaf.

faq.a: A large surface area, a thin barrier (short diffusion distance) and a steep concentration gradient kept by blood flow or ventilation.

faq.q: What makes water move up a tall tree?
faq.a: Transpiration: water evaporates from the leaves and pulls a continuous column of water up the xylem, because water molecules stick together (cohesion–tension).

items.q: Which organ system does the liver belong to?
items.e: The liver is part of the digestive system.

items.q: Which organ system does the lungs belong to?
items.e: The lungs is part of the respiratory system.

items.q: Which level of organisation is the shoot system of a plant?
items.e: The shoot system of a plant is an organ system.

items.q: Which level of organisation is a neuron?
items.e: A neuron is a cell.

items.q: What is the role of bile in digestion?
c: it emulsifies fats into small droplets so lipase can work faster
items.e: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

items.q: How are leaves adapted for gas exchange?
c: stomata and air spaces in the spongy mesophyll
a thick waxy cuticle with no openings
items.e: Guard cells open and close the stomata.

items.q: Which level of organisation is a human?
items.e: A human is an organism.

items.q: Which organ system does the pancreas (making insulin) belong to?
items.e: The pancreas (making insulin) is part of the endocrine system.

items.q: Which organ system does the bladder belong to?
items.e: The bladder is part of the excretory (urinary) system.

items.q: What is the effect of fibrosis?
c: scar tissue makes the alveoli walls thicker, so diffusion is slower
items.e: Tidal volume also falls.

items.q: What is the role of the epithelium in the alveoli?
c: it is one cell thick, giving a short diffusion pathway
items.e: Capillary walls are also very thin.

items.q: Why do single-celled organisms not need a gas exchange system?
c: they have a large surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion is fast enough
items.e: Larger organisms need specialised surfaces.

items.q: What is the counter-current system in fish gills?
c: water and blood flow the same way
blood flows back into the mouth
water and blood flow in opposite directions, keeping a diffusion gradient along the whole lamella
items.e: More oxygen is absorbed than with parallel flow.

items.q: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 8 cm, as x : 1.
Which level of organisation is a root hair cell?
items.e: A root hair cell is a cell.

items.q: Which level of organisation is a skin cell?
items.e: A skin cell is a cell.

items.q: Which level of organisation is a red blood cell?
items.e: A red blood cell is a cell.

items.q: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker wall than the right ventricle?
c: it pumps blood all round the body, which needs higher pressure
it receives blood from the lungs
items.e: The right ventricle pumps only to the lungs.

items.q: What are the products of fat digestion?
items.e: Lipase breaks down lipids.

items.q: Many Australian plants, such as eucalyptus, have tough leaves that hang vertically. How does this help?
c: it lets the plant absorb more water through its leaves
it reduces heating and water loss in strong midday sun
items.e: Hanging leaves receive less direct midday sun.

items.q: Which change increases the rate of transpiration?
items.e: Evaporation is faster in dry, warm, moving air.

items.q: Why does the ileum have villi and microvilli?
c: to give a large surface area for absorption
items.e: Villi also have a good blood supply.

items.q: A block of agar is 1 cm × 4 cm × 10 cm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio, as x : 1.
Pulmonary ventilation is 45.0 L min⁻¹ at 30 breaths per minute. Calculate the tidal volume.
items.e: Tidal volume = ventilation ÷ breathing rate = 1.50 L.

items.q: What shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right?
c: high pCO₂, high H⁺ (low pH) and high temperature
items.e: Oxygen is released more easily in tissues.

items.q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart at high pressure?
items.e: Arteries have thick, elastic walls.

items.q: What is emphysema?
c: a disease in which the alveolar walls are damaged, reducing the surface area
items.e: Cigarette smoking is a major cause.

items.q: How is most carbon dioxide carried in the blood?
items.e: 20–25% is carbaminohaemoglobin and about 7% is dissolved.

items.q: A block of agar is 2 cm × 4 cm × 8 cm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio, as x : 1.
How are the villi of the small intestine adapted?
c: they have a large surface area, thin walls and many capillaries
they release digestive enzymes into the blood
items.e: Microvilli increase the area further.

items.q: A person has a tidal volume of 0.55 L and breathes 12 times per minute. Calculate the pulmonary ventilation rate.
items.e: Pulmonary ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate = 6.60 L min⁻¹.

items.q: What is cell differentiation?
c: a cell becoming specialised for one function by switching on particular genes
a cell losing all its DNA
items.e: All body cells have the same genes but use different ones.

items.q: Which enzyme in red blood cells converts CO₂ and water to carbonic acid?
items.e: It is very fast.

items.q: A person has a tidal volume of 2.0 L and breathes 18 times per minute. Calculate the pulmonary ventilation rate.
items.e: Pulmonary ventilation = tidal volume × breathing rate = 36.0 L min⁻¹.

items.q: Which enzyme breaks down proteins in the stomach?
c: pepsin, a protease that works best in acid
items.e: Stomach acid gives a pH of about 2.

items.q: Pulmonary ventilation is 22.5 L min⁻¹ at 30 breaths per minute. Calculate the tidal volume.
items.e: Tidal volume = ventilation ÷ breathing rate = 0.750 L.

items.q: Which instrument measures lung volumes?
items.e: It traces a spirogram.

items.q: Where does gas exchange take place in the lungs?
items.e: Their walls are one cell thick.

items.q: What is the sigmoid curve that plots % saturation of haemoglobin against pO₂ called?
items.e: It is S-shaped.

items.q: What does phloem carry?
c: water from roots to leaves only
sugars and other organic substances, in both directions (translocation)
items.e: Sieve tubes and companion cells.

items.q: Stroke volume is 90 mL and heart rate is 120 beats per minute. Calculate cardiac output in L min⁻¹.
items.e: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 10800 mL min⁻¹ = 10.8 L min⁻¹.

items.q: Cardiac output is 3.84 L min⁻¹ and stroke volume is 60 mL. Calculate the heart rate.
items.e: HR = CO ÷ SV = 3840 ÷ 60 = 64 beats min⁻¹.

items.q: How do guard cells control water loss?
c: they change shape to open or close the stomata
they pump water into the xylem
items.e: Stomata close when the plant is short of water.

items.q: Stroke volume is 80 mL and heart rate is 64 beats per minute. Calculate cardiac output in L min⁻¹.
items.e: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 5120 mL min⁻¹ = 5.12 L min⁻¹.

items.q: Cardiac output is 13.2 L min⁻¹ and stroke volume is 110 mL. Calculate the heart rate.
items.e: HR = CO ÷ SV = 13200 ÷ 110 = 120 beats min⁻¹.

items.q: Stroke volume is 120 mL and heart rate is 80 beats per minute. Calculate cardiac output in L min⁻¹.
items.e: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 9600 mL min⁻¹ = 9.60 L min⁻¹.

items.q: Why is the curve of an organism living at high altitude shifted to the left?
c: its haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen, so it loads at lower partial pressures
items.e: Llamas and fetal haemoglobin show this.

items.q: Why do capillaries have walls one cell thick?
c: to give a short diffusion distance
items.e: Exchange with tissue fluid happens here.

items.q: How are alveoli adapted for gas exchange?
c: a huge surface area, walls one cell thick and a rich blood supply
items.e: Short diffusion distance and a steep gradient.

items.q: Stroke volume is 100 mL and heart rate is 150 beats per minute. Calculate cardiac output in L min⁻¹.
items.e: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 15000 mL min⁻¹ = 15.0 L min⁻¹.

items.q: Cardiac output is 19.8 L min⁻¹ and heart rate is 180 beats per minute. Calculate the stroke volume in mL.
One cardiac cycle on an ECG lasts 0.60 s. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute.
items.e: Heart rate = 60 ÷ 0.60 = 100 beats min⁻¹.

items.q: Why is the oxygen dissociation curve S-shaped?
c: binding the first oxygen changes the shape and makes it easier for more to bind (cooperative binding)
items.e: The curve is steepest in the middle.

items.q: Cardiac output is 9.60 L min⁻¹ and heart rate is 80 beats per minute. Calculate the stroke volume in mL.
Why do veins have valves?
c: to stop blood flowing backwards at low pressure
items.e: Skeletal muscles squeeze veins.

items.q: Cardiac output is 7.20 L min⁻¹ and stroke volume is 120 mL. Calculate the heart rate.
items.e: HR = CO ÷ SV = 7200 ÷ 120 = 60 beats min⁻¹.

items.q: What is the double circulation of mammals?
c: blood moves in both directions in each vessel
blood passes through the heart twice in each full circuit: to the lungs and to the body
blood goes to the lungs twice
items.e: It keeps pressure high in the body circuit.

items.q: Cardiac output is 7.70 L min⁻¹ and stroke volume is 110 mL. Calculate the heart rate.
items.e: HR = CO ÷ SV = 7700 ÷ 110 = 70 beats min⁻¹.

items.q: What is an atheroma?
c: a blood clot in a vein
a fatty deposit in an artery wall
items.e: It can lead to thrombosis and heart attacks.

items.q: One cardiac cycle on an ECG lasts 0.50 s. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute.
items.e: Heart rate = 60 ÷ 0.50 = 120 beats min⁻¹.

items.q: Which food molecule does amylase break down?
items.e: Amylase → starch, protease → proteins, lipase → lipids.

items.q: What does the trachea contain to keep it open?
items.e: The cartilage is C-shaped.

items.q: A block of agar is 1 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio, as x : 1.
What does xylem carry in a plant?
c: water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves
sugars from the leaves to the roots
items.e: Xylem vessels are dead, hollow tubes.

items.q: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 3 cm, as x : 1.
Which enzyme digests proteins in the stomach?
items.e: It works best in acid conditions.

items.q: Which food molecule does protease break down?
items.e: Amylase → starch, protease → proteins, lipase → lipids.

items.q: Which enzyme breaks down proteins?
items.e: Amylase → starch, protease → proteins, lipase → lipids.

items.q: Which digestive enzyme breaks down starch?
items.e: Amylase is made in the salivary glands and pancreas.

items.q: What is tidal volume?
c: the volume left after breathing out
the maximum volume of the lungs
the volume of air breathed in or out in one normal breath
items.e: About 0.5 L at rest.

items.q: Why are digested food molecules such as glucose absorbed by active transport as well as diffusion?
c: so they can be absorbed even when their concentration in the gut is lower than in the blood
because they are too big to diffuse
items.e: Active transport works against the gradient.

items.q: Which food molecule does lipase break down?
items.e: Amylase → starch, protease → proteins, lipase → lipids.

items.q: What does amylase break starch down into?
items.e: Big molecules are broken into small ones that can be absorbed.

items.q: Why are alveoli efficient gas exchange surfaces?
c: a large surface area, thin walls and a good blood supply
items.e: Ventilation keeps a steep gradient.

items.q: Why do multicellular organisms need transport systems?
c: each cell can make its own oxygen
they have a larger surface area to volume ratio than single cells
their small surface area to volume ratio means diffusion alone is too slow
their cells do not need nutrients
items.e: Blood and xylem carry materials over long distances.

items.q: What is the role of the lacteal in a villus?
c: it absorbs glucose into the blood
it absorbs fatty acids and glycerol into the lymph
items.e: Each villus has a lacteal and capillaries.

items.q: What does lipase break lipids (fats and oils) down into?
items.e: Big molecules are broken into small ones that can be absorbed.

items.q: Why are gill filaments covered in lamellae?
c: to increase the surface area for gas exchange
items.e: Each lamella has many capillaries.

items.q: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube with sides of 4 cm, as x : 1.
Which enzyme digests starch to maltose?
items.e: Made in the salivary glands and pancreas.

items.q: In 10 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 50 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0.50 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0.50² × 50 = 39.3 mm³; ÷ 10 min = 3.93 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: In 2 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 12 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0.60 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0.60² × 12 = 13.6 mm³; ÷ 2 min = 6.79 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: In 2 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 20 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0.25 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0.25² × 20 = 3.93 mm³; ÷ 2 min = 1.96 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: What does phloem transport?
items.e: This is translocation.

items.q: What is the correct order of organisation in a multicellular organism?
items.e: Specialised cells form tissues.

items.q: In 2 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 40 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0.40 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0.40² × 40 = 20.1 mm³; ÷ 2 min = 10.1 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: In 2 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 24 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0.25 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0.25² × 24 = 4.71 mm³; ÷ 2 min = 2.36 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: In 10 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 15 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0.75 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0.75² × 15 = 26.5 mm³; ÷ 10 min = 2.65 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: What is a stem cell?
c: a cell found only in plant stems
an unspecialised cell that can divide and become specialised cells
items.e: Embryonic stem cells can form any cell type.

items.q: Why is lignin present in xylem walls?
c: it strengthens the vessels so they do not collapse
items.e: Xylem vessels are dead with no end walls.

items.q: In 10 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 40 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0.75 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0.75² × 40 = 70.7 mm³; ÷ 10 min = 7.07 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: What does a potometer actually measure?
c: water uptake, which is close to the rate of transpiration
items.e: Some water is used in photosynthesis.

items.q: What is the mass flow hypothesis?
c: sucrose loaded at the source lowers water potential, water enters and pressure pushes the sap to the sink
items.e: Sinks include roots and growing tips.

items.q: What is the cohesion–tension theory?
c: root pressure pushes all water up
water evaporating from leaves pulls a continuous column of water up the xylem
items.e: Hydrogen bonds hold the water molecules together.

items.q: In 10 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 18 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0.60 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0.60² × 18 = 20.4 mm³; ÷ 10 min = 2.04 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: In 2 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 20 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0.60 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0.60² × 20 = 22.6 mm³; ÷ 2 min = 11.3 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: In 2 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 18 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0.60 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 0.60² × 18 = 20.4 mm³; ÷ 2 min = 10.2 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: In 6 minutes an air bubble in a potometer moves 12 mm along a capillary tube of radius 1.0 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.e: Volume = πr²d = π × 1.0² × 12 = 37.7 mm³; ÷ 6 min = 6.28 mm³ min⁻¹.

items.q: What is transpiration?
c: the loss of water vapour from the leaves through the stomata
items.e: It pulls water up the xylem.

items.q: Why must a potometer be set up under water?
c: to stop air entering the xylem and the apparatus
items.e: An airlock would stop the water column.
